items.actClause: AN ACT to amend chapter 507 of the laws of 1974, relating to providing for the apportionment of state monies to certain nonpublic schools, to reimburse them for their expenses in complying with certain state requirements for the administration of state testing and evaluation programs and for participation in state programs for the reporting of basic educational data, in relation to the calculation of nonpublic schools' eligibility to receive aid
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S6089

 TITLE OF BILL :

An act to amend chapter 507 of the laws of 1974, relating to providing
for the apportionment of state monies to certain nonpublic schools, to
reimburse them for their expenses in complying with certain state
requirements for the administration of state testing and evaluation
programs and for participation in state programs for the reporting of
basic educational data, in relation to the calculation of nonpublic
schools' eligibility to receive aid

 PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL :

To clarify that the State Education Department may continue to utilize
the instructional time standard as the basis for providing
reimbursement to nonpublic schools for their participation in the
mandated services aid program.

 SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS :

Section 3 of chapter 507 of the laws of 1974 is amended to clarify
that schools will continue to be eligible for reimbursement based on
the instructional time standard utilized historically by department.
Section 2 provides for an immediate effective date in order that the
department may process reimbursement claims currently being held.

 EXISTING LAW :

Except for 2016 appropriation language, existing law has been silent
on the issue. Nonetheless, this legislation codifies the long-standing
reimbursement standard.

 JUSTIFICATION :

For more than 30 years, the State Education Department has used the
instructional time standard (an approx.180 day instructional school
year and a 5 / 5.5 hour instructional day) as the basis for aid to
most nonpublic schools under the Mandated Services Aid program. The
"instructional time" standard, which is also used as the basis for aid
to public schools, is tied to the provisions of the compulsory
education law and helps to provide consistency and predictability in
aid to schools.

In recent years, a number of nonpublic schools began receiving less
aid based on the department having adjusted the reimbursement
standards for those schools. Aid to most schools, however, continued
without reductions. In the 2016-2017 State Budget, language was
enacted to continue the historic practice of using "instructional
hours" in the day but it did not address the number of "instructional
days" in the year. Despite both houses having included the language
relating to "instructional days" in their one-house budgets this
session - it was not included in the final budget.

The proposed language clarifies that reimbursement may continue based
on both the number of days as well as the number of hours of
instructional time. By defining the days as those on which attendance
is taken, schools will be required to also include days (or the
portion of days) during which tests are being administered.

The legislation is necessary to avoid a reduction in reimbursement to
nonpublic schools.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

None
 STATE FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :

Up to $6 million if schools whose reimbursement was reduced in prior
years are permitted to return to using the instructional time
standard.

 LOCAL FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :

Will help keep school reimbursement from being reduced.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
The act shall take effect immediately.

items.memoText:
VETO MESSAGE - No. 236
 
TO THE SENATE:
 
I am returning herewith, without my approval, the following bills:
 
Senate Bill number 2482-C, entitled:
 
    "AN  ACT  to  amend  the  education law, in relation to the New York
      state masters-in-education teacher incentive scholarship program"
 
Senate Bill number 6089, entitled:
 
    "AN ACT to amend chapter 507  of  the  laws  of  1974,  relating  to
      providing for the apportionment of state monies to certain nonpub-
      lic  schools,  to  reimburse  them for their expenses in complying
      with certain state requirements for the  administration  of  state
      testing  and  evaluation  programs  and for participation in state
      programs for the reporting of basic educational data, in  relation
      to  the  calculation  of nonpublic schools' eligibility to receive
      aid"
 
TO THE ASSEMBLY:
 
I am returning herewith, without my approval, the following bills:
 
Assembly Bill number 934-A, entitled:
 
    "AN ACT to amend the education law, in relation to  state  appropri-
      ations to the state university of New York and the city university
      of New York"
 
Assembly Bill number 967, entitled:
 
    "AN  ACT  to  amend  the state finance law, in relation to five-year
      capital plans for the state university of New York  and  the  city
      university of New York"
 
Assembly Bill number 1808-A, entitled:
 
    "AN  ACT  to  amend  the  education law, in relation to the New York
      state science, technology, engineering and  mathematics  incentive
      program"
 
Assembly Bill number 7697, entitled:
 
    "AN  ACT  to  amend  the  education law, in relation to the enhanced
      tuition awards"
 
    NOT APPROVED

  New York's education system  and  its  investments  in  education  are
unparalleled.  The  2017-2018  Budget  increased  Education Aid for K-12
education by $1.1 billion. During the past  six  years  of  my  Adminis-
tration,  the  State's  funding  for  Education  Aid  has increased $6.2
billion, or 32 percent. New York State now leads the nation in  spending
per pupil on K-12 education.
 
  At  the  same time, my Administration has made significant investments
in support of higher education institutions and  student  financial  aid
programs,  increasing  funding  by  $1.3  billion,  or  22  percent. The
2017-2018 Budget provides a record $7.5 billion  in  total  support  for
higher education, a $448 million, or 6.3 percent increase over the prior
year. New York State also provides more funding to independent (private)
higher education institutions than any state except one.
 
  My  commitment  to  funding  education  at  all  levels is unwavering.
Collectively, however, these bills would add  hundreds  of  millions  of
dollars in increased and unbudgeted costs to the State's financial plan,
which  will  ultimately  be  shouldered  by  the State's taxpayers. Such
education funding decisions, both in terms  of  revenues  available  and
appropriations  to be expended, have always been, and should continue to
be, addressed in the context of the annual  budget  negotiations.  At  a
time  when  the Federal government has enacted, and is threatening addi-
tional, devastating cuts to the State,  it  would  be  irresponsible  to
incur such unbudgeted costs at this time.
 
  Moreover,  these  bills  would  violate  existing agreements that were
previously negotiated with the Legislature during the budget negotiation
process. There is no reason  to  violate  these  negotiated  agreements,
especially  when it would place an unnecessary and significant strain on
State resources. For these reasons,  I  am  constrained  to  veto  these
bills.
 
  These bills are disapproved.                (signed) ANDREW M. CUOMO
 
                               __________
